articles.title: Trump weighs moving White House press corps out of building
articles.summary: Outside allies of President Trump have recently pushed the idea of moving the White House press corps to another building, including former Trump strategist...
articles.body:
President Trump has discussed the possibility of moving the White House press corps to another building, according to two people close to the president — a move that could escalate Mr. Trump's clashes with news organizations over coverage and access.

Outside allies of the president have pushed the idea in recent weeks, including former Trump strategist Steve Bannon, one source told CBS News.

No final decisions have been made, according to both sources.

The discussions were first reported by The New York Times .

White House communications director Steven Cheung said in a statement: "America is rightly distrustful of the fake news media because they fabricate stories based off lies and sources who are not even privy to any type of information. … All options remain on the table, and we will make an announcement when appropriate."

Reporters have had dedicated workspaces in the White House building for more than a century. The current press briefing room was constructed during the Nixon administration , replacing a swimming pool that dated back to Franklin D. Roosevelt's presidency.

But late last month, Mr. Trump posted a before-and-after image to Truth Social that suggested the briefing room could be turned back into a swimming pool.

Ahead of Mr. Trump's first term, administration officials floated the idea of moving the press corps out of the building, framing it as a bid to broaden access by using a roomier part of the White House complex rather than the small, cramped spaces in the West Wing. Incoming chief of staff Reince Priebus told NBC News the administration had discussed holding news conferences in the Eisenhower Executive Office Building, which is adjacent to the West Wing.

Mr. Trump ultimately did not follow through with the plans, telling Fox News two days before his 2017 inauguration : "The press went crazy, so I said, 'Let's not move it.'"

The idea has appeared to reemerge after more than a year of disputes between the Trump administration and journalists over access to the White House.

Last month, Mr. Trump attempted to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House complex, accusing them of unfair coverage. Journalists from all three outlets were briefly unable to access the building, but a federal judge reinstated their press credentials , finding the ban likely violated the First Amendment and the news outlets' right to due process.

The Trump administration has continued to periodically block CNN from participating in the television press pool, a group of five networks that cover the president's travel and events on a rotating basis and provide video to other news organizations.

(CNN and CBS News are both part of Skydance, the parent company formed by the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery.)

More than a year ago, the White House prevented the Associated Press from accessing the Oval Office and some other spaces because the wire service declined to refer to the Gulf of Mexico by Mr. Trump's preferred term, the Gulf of America.

The Pentagon has also clamped down on press access. Last year, the military required reporters to sign onto a set of restrictions — including a promise not to "solicit" sensitive information — in order to maintain daily access to the Pentagon. Most news organizations declined to sign the new rules and vacated the building.

After a judge struck down the Pentagon's press restrictions earlier this year, the military announced it would stop allowing reporters to enter the building unescorted altogether.

Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said a "new and improved press workspace will be established in an annex facility outside the Pentagon, but still on Pentagon grounds."

articles.title: Congressional candidate Brad Lander says he was detained by Israeli military in West Bank
articles.summary: New York congressional candidate Brad Lander (D) said Wednesday he was detained by the Israeli military in the West Bank while “harvesting olives in a grove near Nehalim.” “The occupation is a crime under international law. Harvesting olives isn’t a crime under any law I know,” Lander wrote in a post on the social platform…
articles.body:
New York congressional candidate Brad Lander (D) said Wednesday he was detained by the Israeli military in the West Bank while “harvesting olives in a grove near Nehalim.”

“The occupation is a crime under international law. Harvesting olives isn’t a crime under any law I know,” Lander wrote in a post on the social platform X .

In a post on Monday , Lander said he was in the West Bank with the Protect the Harvest coalition, which he said was bringing people together from around the world to help Palestinian farmers harvest olives.

He posted an update the next day with a video attachment of him speaking with Amira Musallam from an advocacy group called Unarmed Civilian Protection in Palestine, who described an alleged attack by Israeli settlers in a house near the olive grove the group harvested that day.

Lander, the former New York City comptroller , is running against Republican candidate Jennifer Moore in New York’s 10th Congressional District. He defeated incumbent Rep. Dan Goldman (D) in the Democratic primary earlier this year.

The Hill has reached out to Lander’s campaign.

This incident comes days after The Washington Post said one of its photojournalists, Heidi Levine, was attacked by Israeli settlers while working on assignment in the West Bank.

The Post shared a video capturing the incident the on social platform X , which appeared to show masked Israeli settlers attacking Levine while she was on the ground.

In a statement following the incident , Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu condemned the attack, saying, “Israel unequivocally condemns violence against anyone—Jews, Arabs, Christians or journalists. Those responsible will be held accountable.”

Netanyahu also raised questions about the encounter in his post saying, “Reports indicate some 200 Arabs and far-left activists confronted approximately 40 Israeli youths.”

articles.title: Thune makes bold prediction about Republicans' Senate chances as GOP pulls millions from key races
articles.summary: John Thune says Republicans will outperform the polls in toss-up senate races despite shifting campaign cash away from Georgia and into Kansas.
articles.body: FREMONT, Neb. — Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., is predicting Republicans will outperform the polls and retain their narrow Senate majority, even as GOP-aligned groups pull millions of dollars from struggling candidates and redirect resources to races that have suddenly become more competitive. Thune has been crisscrossing the country campaigning for vulnerable Republicans ahead of the Nov. 3 election. He’s confident that they can hold onto their slim, 53-to-47-seat majority in the Senate but acknowledges that the GOP as a whole faces headwinds. And as Election Day inches closer and closer, several contests across the country have tightened, like in Kansas, while others may be slipping away from Republicans, like in North Carolina or Georgia. DEMOCRATS THINK A BLUE WAVE IS BUILDING. HERE ARE 3 FORCES THAT COULD STOP IT Thune, in an interview with Fox News Digital on the trail supporting Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., was still optimistic about the GOP’s chances. "I think there are a lot of races right now just looking at the polling that are up for grabs," Thune said. "I mean you could call them jump balls, however you want to say it. They're margin of error races, and there are some that are maybe a little out of the margin. But I do think the polling right now, like it has been in past elections, under-reflects the Republican vote." "And I think you'll see some of that. So we're not giving up on any of them," he continued. Republicans are hoping to defend six toss-up races this cycle, according to Cook Political Report. And several that earlier appeared as safe bets, like Mississippi and South Carolina, have recently shifted more favorably towards Democrats. 12 RACES SCRAMBLE SENATE BATTLEFIELD AS DEMOCRATS EYE COMEBACK The flow of campaign cash has been staggering during this midterm cycle, with Republican political action committees (PACs) and outside groups dumping hundreds of millions of dollars in key races across the country. But where the money is being shifted could be more telling. Earlier this month, the Senate Leadership Fund, a PAC closely aligned with Thune, moved money from Georgia to Kansas, where Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., is locked in one of the more unexpected toss-up contests of the cycle. The Senate Leadership Fund had initially pledged $44 million to bolster Rep. Mike Collins, R-Ga., in his quest to topple Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga. But the incumbent first-term senator has been raking in campaign donations and consistently led Collins in polling. DEMOCRATS SEE NEW CHANCES TO FLIP RED STATES — BUT A $400M GOP SPENDING ADVANTAGE COULD DERAIL THEIR PLANS And in North Carolina, where former Republican National Committee (RNC) co-chair Michael Whatley is running to keep retiring Sen. Thom Tillis’ seat red against former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper, outside funding has begun to dissipate. The Senate Leadership Fund similarly pulled back nearly all of its spending in the state earlier this month, a sign that confidence in Whatley’s ability to best Cooper was waning. Even President Donald Trump, who held a rally for Whatley on Tuesday, is worried about the race. "I think he’s a great man, and I am worried about him," Trump told reporters earlier this month. "I hope he wins. He was a great leader for the whole Republican Party when I won, and he’d be a great senator." Meanwhile, Thune was still bullish that Republicans could hold on, but ultimately, it would come down to getting the "low propensity, particularly Trump, voters out, and then you've got to work on winning the middle of the electorate." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Turnout's going to be a big part of whether or not we're successful or not. And in every state I've been in, that is a clear-eyed focus of our candidates," Thune said. "That's where resources are being invested. And I think that could be the difference for us come Election Day on whether or not we win a lot of these close races or not," he continued. "And I think that we're gonna outperform the polls for sure come Election Day."

articles.title: Trump says he’s requiring data centers to provide their own electricity
articles.summary: President Trump said Wednesday he will require data centers to provide their own electricity and give “any excess” energy to neighboring communities to prevent rising electrical costs. “As the President of the United States, I have been watching Data Centers very closely, and have come to a very strong conclusion,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.…
articles.body:
President Trump said Wednesday he will require data centers to provide their own electricity and give “any excess” energy to neighboring communities to prevent rising electrical costs.

“As the President of the United States, I have been watching Data Centers very closely, and have come to a very strong conclusion,” Trump wrote on Truth Social . “New and large, in some cases gigantic, Data Centers are mandated by me to make their own electricity, and give or sell any excess back to the local community, or grid, and therefore there is electric price increase.”

“In fact, there could be a substantial decrease. Other elements likewise!” Trump continued.

The president added that , while data centers have been “highly unpopular in a certain area,” they are “extremely popular when a financial deal is struck.”

“MAKE DEA L S, and get them built!!!” he concluded.

Tech companies have argued, in line with Trump’s embrace of establishing AI infrastructure, that establishing data centers is necessary to support the emerging technology’s development. Dozens of companies — such as Meta, Amazon and Google — have agreed to pay for increased energy costs caused by their data centers through Trump’s ratepayer protection pledge.

A medium-sized data center can consume up to about 110 million gallons of water per year for cooling purposes, equivalent to the annual water usage of roughly 1,000 households, according to an analysis by the nonprofit Environmental and Energy Study Institute last year .

The president claimed last month that critics of data centers want “ poverty, crime and squalor .” He accused communities against data centers of wanting to be “ backwards and poor .” Earlier this month, amid a tight Senate race in Ohio, Trump emphasized how “much money” the state would make , as some Ohioans criticized the data center development.

“You can’t just turn them off. They’ll go to China,” Trump said at a rally for Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio), whom opponents in the Buckeye State have criticized for wanting to bring data centers to Ohio while serving as lieutenant governor.

Americans have grown wary of such projects over concerns they could result in higher electricity costs, strain water resources and produce noise or air pollution. Some communities have seen greater tax revenue brought in by data centers , while others used tax breaks to attract investments.

States including Ohio and Illinois have paused such tax incentive programs in recent months, while others have moved even more aggressively. New York instituted the nation’s first statewide freeze on new “hyperscale” data centers.

The push against AI has also been driven by concerns over the risks posed by rogue software, particularly after recent attempted and successful hacks into government websites. These fears also come following a warning from former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon that AI could become an existential threat to humanity by the end of the decade.

articles.title: Trump approval at new lows in polling days before midterms
articles.summary: President Trump’s approval ratings have hit new lows shortly before this year’s midterms, according to fresh polls from The New York Times/Siena University and CNN. In the Times/Siena poll, 36 percent of respondents said they either “strongly approve” or “somewhat approve” of Trump’s job performance, while another 59 percent said they either “somewhat disapprove” or…
articles.body:
President Trump’s approval ratings have hit new lows shortly before this year’s midterms, according to fresh polls from The New York Times/Siena University and CNN.

In the Times/Siena poll , 36 percent of respondents said they either “strongly approve” or “somewhat approve” of Trump’s job performance, while another 59 percent said they either “somewhat disapprove” or “strongly disapprove.” Five percent didn’t respond or were unsure about how they felt about Trump’s job performance.

The Times reported Tuesday that Trump’s 36 percent approval was a record low for all Times/Siena polls.

In the CNN poll , 32 percent of respondents said they either “approve strongly” or “approve moderately” of Trump’s job performance, while sixty-seven percent of respondents said they either “disapprove strongly” or “disapprove moderately.” CNN also reported Tuesday that Trump’s approval rating in the poll was historically low .

Both polls come less than two weeks out from this year’s midterms, in which Trump and Republicans are facing an uphill battle due to issues like the unpopular Iran war, concerns about the cost of living, gas prices and the president’s own unpopularity.

According to a polling average from Decision Desk HQ, Trump’s approval rating was sitting at 39.2 percent on Wednesday morning, while his disapproval rating was 59.1 percent.

Energy concerns are also a key issue in this year’s midterms, with the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for the oil industry, closed amid the Iran war. The strait’s closure has driven up oil and gas prices, with the average cost of a gallon of regular gas in the U.S. at about $4.26 on Wednesday morning , up from about $3.05 last year at the same time.

The CNN poll took place from Oct. 15 to 18, featuring 1,701 people and a margin of error of 2.9 percentage points. The Times/Siena poll took place from Oct. 12 to 19 and featured 3,494 voters and a margin of error of 1.9 percentage points.

articles.title: Menopause is having its overdue moment
articles.summary: This shift is urgently needed.
articles.body:
Congress recently convened a first-ever hearing on menopause. That it took this long for lawmakers to address this important issue mirrors how we as a nation have failed to publicly confront, thoughtfully study and allocate meaningful federal funding to address this predictable stage of women’s health.

Last month, Sens. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.) and Rick Scott (R-Fla.) invited physicians and experts to testify before Congress on the current state of menopause training, research and care. Their collective assessment was discouraging — physician shortages, inadequate access to care, insurance challenges and a lack of medical education were cited among many reasons why there’s been little progress.

The senators also asked the Government Accountability Office to examine how the federal government has funded menopause research to identify gaps in training, treatment and oversight.

Menopause is the normal part of a woman’s aging process that marks the end of her reproductive years. A major hormonal shift takes place, often triggering hot flashes, night sweats, sleep interruption, emotional swings, urinary changes, concentration loss, weight gain and headaches. These symptoms, if left untreated, can be enormously challenging for women and their families.

Menopause is a biological reality that roughly half of the U.S. population will experience. These women will spend as much as one-third of their lives in perimenopause and menopause. Yet, for generations, it has occupied a taboo place in our culture.

Because it’s a topic no one wants to talk about.

The problem begins, in part, with medical training and education. Menopause isn’t prioritized as a field of study among obstetricians and gynecologists. One survey of U.S. OB-GYN residency programs found that just over 30 percent had a menopause curriculum.

The Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education requires that an OB-GYN in training must log a minimum of 360 direct deliveries . Today, there is no such standard required for doctors treating menopause.

Women often consult primary care physicians as perimenopausal symptoms develop, and there are significant gaps in menopause knowledge among clinicians who practice internal medicine. A lack of training is among the most frequently cited barriers to providing quality menopause care globally.

A woman in menopause experiencing insomnia, brain fog or hot flashes, or any one of a myriad of normal menopausal symptoms, can find herself in an extremely difficult situation. She is going through a normal transition, yet because of unfair gender stereotypes, she can jeopardize her standing in the workplace if she talks about it openly.

Most companies have policies addressing pregnancy, disability and other health conditions. But in the U.S., menopause remains largely absent from workplace planning, even though symptoms such as sleep disruption and concentration loss can affect productivity, retention and advancement.

That stands in stark contrast to the United Kingdom, where companies that employ over 250 people are legally required to publish annual Menopause Action Plans for the purpose of “ building equitable, productive workplaces .”

For many women, perimenopause occurs during high earning years at a time when women have more experience and time to give to their careers. One study put menopause’s total annual cost to the U.S. economy at nearly $27 billion.

And there are added complications for women who have survived cancer. Hormone replacement therapy can be a helpful treatment for some women experiencing menopausal symptoms but is often not recommended for breast cancer survivors as it may heighten the risk of recurrence. This is especially alarming as 1 in 8 women in America will develop breast cancer.

That’s why congressional calls for more research and training matter. Women deserve treatment options based on evidence — not guesswork from physicians.

The medical community is responding to the heightened interest in menopause. Days ago, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists refreshed its recommendations on menopause treatment options. Its last update was reportedly 12 years ago.

Awareness is also critical. In April, comedian Amy Schumer became the face of Midi Health’s national “ Midlife Back in Session ” campaign, using humor to talk openly about menopause symptoms ranging from hot flashes to mood changes.

And legislation to improve federal funding for menopause is underway. This spring, Sens. Patty Murray (D-Wash.) and Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) introduced the Advancing Care and Mid-life Women’s Health Act, which would authorize $275 million for training, education and research. Combined, these efforts can move menopause from the sidelines of U.S. women’s health policy to the mainstream of medical education, research funding and workplace practice.

This shift is urgently needed. Because every woman deserves to enter menopause equipped with accurate information, delivered by trained medical professionals and have the ability to talk about it openly, without fear of being judged or burdened by misguided feelings of shame or embarrassment.

Lyndon Haviland, DrPH, MPH, is a distinguished scholar at the CUNY School of Public Health and Health Policy.

articles.title: ‘The President is not popular’: GOP candidate cuts apparent AI prompt from website
articles.summary: A Republican candidate in Minnesota has deleted a phrase from his campaign website stating that President Trump is unpopular, a mention that appeared to be a prompt given to AI to generate a message for the candidate. Eric Pratt, running in Minnesota’s 2nd Congressional District, initially included an instructional phrase about how to craft a…
articles.body:
A Republican candidate in Minnesota has deleted a phrase from his campaign website stating that President Trump is unpopular, a mention that appeared to be a prompt given to AI to generate a message for the candidate.

Eric Pratt, running in Minnesota’s 2nd Congressional District, initially included an instructional phrase about how to craft a message on affordability.

“Residents want everyday purchases to be affordable, bad actors to be held accountable, and for their reps to lead with common sense,” the website read. “The President is not popular, so all messaging should be focused on local politics and needs.”

The first sentence remains on his site, but the prompt about the president has been deleted.

Pratt’s apparent blunder went viral online, and an archive of the website on the Wayback Machine reviewed by The Hill confirms the phrase was included.

In a statement to The Hill, a Pratt campaign spokesperson accused Minnesota Democrats of using the prompt to distract from the campaign’s central issues.

“While Eric is focused on representing the residents of the Second Congressional District, the DFL wants to make this race about anything but the issues that actually matter here: making life more affordable, holding people accountable, and keeping our communities safe,” the campaign said. “Instead, they focus on an internal staff note that was inadvertently included on a website update.”

Republican candidates are increasingly distancing themselves from the president as his popularity reaches record lows ahead of the midterms. A New York Times/Siena University Poll out Wednesday put the president’s approval rating at just 36 percent among likely voters, with 59 percent disapproving.

Some GOP candidates in battleground districts around the country are leaving off mentions of Trump on their campaign websites. Even in Florida, where the statewide races lean toward Republicans this cycle, the Republican nominee for governor, Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.), removed several mentions of the president from his website.

Across competitive Senate races, Republicans are calling for an end to the Iran war. Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) and former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), both running for Senate, called for an immediate end to the war, as did Ohio Sen. Jon Husted (R), who is in a tough fight for reelection.

In traditionally Republican Kansas, Sen. Roger Marshall (R), also fighting for reelection, criticized immigration enforcement operations in his state.

Pratt already had long odds to flip Minnesota’s 2nd, an open seat being vacated by Rep. Angie Craig (D). Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ, a partner of The Hill, gives Pratt just a 3 percent chance of defeating Democrat Matt Little.

articles.title: Democrats call for investigation into Musk over reported Starlink slowdown order
articles.summary: Democrats are calling for an investigation into SpaceX CEO Elon Musk following a Wall Street Journal report alleging he ordered the Starlink slowdown in Ukraine. “Either the President was lying or Musk was lying, but the decision to slow down satellite speed and access has life or death consequences for Ukraine,” Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.)…
articles.body:
Democrats are calling for an investigation into SpaceX CEO Elon Musk following a Wall Street Journal report alleging he ordered the Starlink slowdown in Ukraine.

“Either the President was lying or Musk was lying, but the decision to slow down satellite speed and access has life or death consequences for Ukraine,” Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) wrote on social media . “This deserves a full investigation by the Senate. Elon Musk should be compelled to testify before Congress and under oath.”

“National security decisions should be made in our national security interests, and not based on the personal whim of an unstable executive,” Schiff continued.

The slowdown occurred earlier this month, targeting Starlink-supported Ukrainian military drones, airplanes and helicopters traveling faster than 100 mph, a source familiar with the matter previously told The Hill.

Musk — the world’s richest person — initially claimed in a post that only President Trump had the ability to order the slowdown, adding that while Starlink is under Musk’s SpaceX, Starshield is owned and operated by the U.S. government.

In response to the Journal’s report, Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) posted on the social platform X , “@elonmusk you don’t have to wait for a subpoena, you can just come in on your own.”

The move comes as Trump and Musk have been increasingly critical of Ukraine and its president, Volodymyr Zelensky, who said after the slowdown that “ people will die ” and called the move a “big mistake.”

Trump has faced intense pressure from both sides of the aisle for continuing to grow closer to Russian President Vladimir Putin by signing an executive order to waive sanctions on Russian energy and purchasing large quantities of Russian diesel .

Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.) slammed Musk directly in a video on X , saying the SpaceX CEO “shouldn’t have the power to influence the outcome of a war with the flip of a switch. Yet he and Trump seem determined to put their finger on the scale for Putin.”

Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) told CNN’s Kaitlan Collins that there is an “ enormous risk ” if Musk is “dictating our foreign policy” by deciding what tools Ukraine has on the battlefield.

“We’d like to know exactly who is responsible for what happened,” she stated.

articles.title: Ilhan Omar finally emerges after DC raid with video pleading for cash to fight Trump
articles.summary: Ilhan Omar's campaign video breaks her silence after the DHS raid on her D.C. home, accusing Trump of trying to intimidate political enemies.
articles.body: Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., re-emerged Tuesday night for the first time following a raid on her Washington, D.C., residence by posting a campaign video to her official social media channels asking supporters for more money. "Hi everyone, Ilhan here," Omar said in a selfie video showing her riding in the back seat of a vehicle and wearing a blue campaign shirt. "I just wanted to say thank you so much for the support, to everyone who sent a note of support, for everyone who sent $5, $10, $20." Omar's home in Washington, D.C., was raided by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) last Monday in connection to an investigation into potential immigration fraud. Authorities are probing whether Omar or her father lied on paperwork that helped her gain citizenship. Border czar Tom Homan has said that if the allegations are proven, Omar could be denaturalized. She closed her video by pleading for more cash. "Please continue to support us. It's going to be a very expensive and challenging time. So we appreciate whether you're able to send $5, $10, $20. Thank you." ILHAN OMAR'S TURBULENT WEEK EXPLAINED: THE DUELING PROBES THAT THREW THE SOMALI-BORN PROGRESSIVE INTO CHAOS The video showed a partial image of the outside of the window, and while trees and buildings whizzed by, it was not immediately clear from where the congresswoman was shooting the clip. Omar did not directly address the investigation or the raid, but attacked President Donald Trump. She said that the money she received in the fallout from the search "goes a long way as we fight Trump and his administration for trying to intimidate me and so many people right before the midterm elections." "We know that they're running scared," she said of Trump and Republicans heading into a consequential midterm election. "We're not going to be intimidated. We're not going to be silenced. We're not going to be scared." Omar has not been seen publicly since before the raid on her home, which was first reported by Fox News Digital last week. Her husband, Tim Mynett, has been seen outside the residence walking their dog. Additionally, Fox News Digital has spotted a campaign aide bringing in food and both of her daughters arriving at the home two days apart. TRUMP RALLY CROWD CHANTS 'DEPORT' AS PRESIDENT RIPS ILHAN OMAR AFTER FEDERAL RAID The congresswoman's sister, Sahra Noor, is in the U.S. on a book tour and spoke with federal investigators last week in the wake of the raid, three sources confirmed to Fox News Digital. Omar promised in her clip posted Tuesday night to get back on the campaign trail as the midterms rapidly approach. "I'll be out there campaigning alongside all of you, and making sure that we beat back all of this, and that we win in the midterms," she said. "Win the House, win the Senate, and hold this administration accountable." She is currently scheduled to appear in Minneapolis on Monday for a live show with radical left-wing streamer Hasan Piker. It is unclear where Omar is, or has been, since the search warrant was executed last Monday. Some speculated that she fled the country — though reports note that her passport and phone were among the items seized by federal agents during the raid. ILHAN OMAR'S HUSBAND SNAPS OVER RUMORS SHE FLED US AFTER FEDERAL IMMIGRATION FRAUD RAID Before posting the video on Tuesday, Omar had only released written statements on social media. "This raid by Trump’s DHS is an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies," she said in a statement posted to X hours after feds descended on her home. "For a decade, Donald Trump has relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Ilhan Omar with inflammatory rhetoric, repeatedly putting a target on her back," the post continued. "Now, those attacks have escalated to a pointless federal raid. The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong. No president should be able to use the power of the federal government to intimidate his political enemies." HOMAN SAYS ILHAN OMAR COULD BE STRIPPED OF NATURALIZATION, DEPORTED IF IMMIGRATION FRAUD IS PROVEN Trump warned Tuesday from the Oval Office that Omar could be jailed if the allegations against her are true. "Well, she could be. She could also go to jail," Trump said. "You know, they keep talking about deportation. No, she could go to jail." "This is just my opinion," he continued, before calling the congresswoman "a very dishonest person" who "hates our country." articles.title: Supreme Court rejects Trump policy restricting treatment for transgender federal inmates
articles.summary: The Supreme Court on Wednesday said the Trump administration cannot enforce a new policy that restricts treatment for transgender inmates in federal prison.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Wednesday said the Trump administration cannot enforce a new policy that restricts treatment for transgender inmates in federal prison. The justices in a brief order rejected an emergency application filed by the administration that sought to block a lower court injunction against the proposal. There are about 1,000 transgender inmates in federal custody. The policy is part of President Donald Trump’s broader effort to roll back moves to expand transgender rights. It was announced in line with his January 2025 executive order telling federal agencies not to acknowledge the concept of gender identity outside of the “immutable biological classification” of male or female. The court order included no explanation, saying only that two conservative justices, Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito, would have granted it. In several different announcements, the Bureau of Prisons over the last 18 months has said it will not provide gender transition surgery, hormone treatments or “social accommodations” such as wigs, padding or makeup. That rolled back previous policies that allowed for gender-affirming care, with the government saying that such treatments have recently been called into question by medical professionals. That claim is heavily contested by transgender rights advocates. If the policy had gone into effect, the only treatment transgender inmates would have been able to receive would be mental health services and potentially medications like antidepressants. A group of transgender inmates sued, with the backing of the American Civil Liberties Union, arguing the government had failed to adequately explain the change. They also alleged a violation of the Constitution’s Eighth Amendment, which bars cruel and unusual punishment. The lead plaintiffs in the case, Alishea Kingdom, Jas Kapule and Solo Nichols, have all been receiving hormone treatment for several years. Washington-based U.S. District Judge Royce Lamberth blocked the current policy in a ruling earlier this year, concluding that the Bureau of Prisons had failed to consider the merits of its past treatment of transgender inmates in formulating the plan. “Despite providing gender-affirming care to inmates in its custody for years, the government cites in the Program Statement zero evidence from its own medical or mental health professionals to support its conclusions,” he wrote. The government provided no evidence that the previous plan was “ineffective or harmful,” he added. Lamberth, a Reagan appointee, also found that the proposal appeared to be engineered precisely to comply with the president’s executive order, concluding that the reasons given were pretextual. In September, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit rejected a Trump administration request seeking to block the judge’s final decision, with the panel split 2-1. In court papers, Solicitor General D. John Sauer said the lower court was guilty of “substituting its own policy judgment for that of the agency” and was essentially faulting the Bureau of Prisons for following the president’s executive order. ACLU lawyers said in court papers that the Bureau of Prisons has provided hormone therapy to inmates since 1992 while also gradually expanding access to other treatments and social accommodations. The abrupt change without necessary explanation “gives rise to the inference that the agency’s purported reasons were not its actual reasons,” the lawyers wrote. “That glaring omission, as well as the unreasonableness of its decision, make it clear that the rationales were contrived to support the demand President Trump made” in the executive order. The case marks a rare recent win for transgender advocates at the Supreme Court, which has a 6-3 conservative majority. In June, the court upheld state bans on transgender athletes seeking to participate in women’s and girls’ sports. A year earlier, the court backed state laws banning gender transition treatments for transgender youths. The court has also allowed Trump to implement a ban on transgender people in the military.

articles.title: Democrats furious after pollster boosting far-left candidates admits fabricating surveys: ‘Absolute scumbags’
articles.summary: Wedgewood Polling admitted to fabricating data, shaking key races including the Michigan Senate primary between Abdul El-Sayed and Mallory McMorrow.
articles.body: Democrats are up in arms after a so-called polling firm that projected far-left candidates as strong contenders in several primaries admitted that it had fabricated its polling data. Wedgewood Polling, which billed itself as an election survey company, released a statement Tuesday night admitting it used "fabricated numbers" for an "experimental project to demonstrate the vulnerabilities, lack of oversight, and overall low barrier to entry in the modern political polling industry." The group's polls were cited by Abdul El-Sayed's campaign amid a high-profile primary race against Michigan state Sen. Mallory McMorrow and U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich. The nonpartisan polling aggregator Political Polls also cited Wedgewood in the Wisconsin gubernatorial race, showing socialist Francesca Hong having an edge over Republican candidate Rep. Tom Tiffany, R-Wis. McMorrow said Wedgewood's numbers led to her donations drying up and reporters having "hounded" her with calls to drop out of the race. JONATHAN TURLEY: FAKE POLLSTER'S STUNT WAS A RECKLESS GAME WITH REAL RACES "Sure, a point was proven. Polling is broken. But tens of thousands of people poured their hearts, time, energy, hard-earned money into something they believed in - for a year-and-a-half, and it was treated like a game," she said in a statement on X. "Trust is already at an all-time low. We don't get out of this mess without rebuilding trust. And media - who loves to ride the drama of a pollercoaster - needs to take a hard look at what's legitimate and what's not." Unlike El-Sayed, who advanced from Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary, Hong lost Wisconsin’s Democratic gubernatorial primary to the establishment-backed candidate. El-Sayed, a former Michigan public health official, is currently locked in a tight race against former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers, R-Mich., for Michigan's open Senate seat. Democrat strategist Jennifer Holdsworth said she ran a super PAC that raised money for McMorrow and that "this poll was used by several donors to pull back funding at a time we were being outspent by $80 million." MORNING GLORY: THE POLLS GOT MICHIGAN BADLY WRONG. NOW DEMOCRATS MAY FACE A BIGGER RECKONING Wedgewood's numbers were cited by high-profile outlets like The New York Times and Decision Desk HQ, which both said they have since removed them from their projections. The Times said it removed 15 polls released by Wedgewood between June and October after it admitted to fabricating data. The outlet said Wedgewood had "answered a series of questions regarding the identities of the pollsters; the methods they were using to draw their sample, contact respondents and weight their polls; and the source of their funding" during its vetting process. Decision Desk HQ said it removed 17 Wedgewood polls from its projections but that it "has not changed the projected seat totals or chamber control probabilities in the Senate or House." Wedgewood Polling's statement said it "was never intended to sway an election" but rather was aimed as a "wake-up call" about data integrity and vetting standards. MYSTERIOUS POLLING FIRM BEHIND FAKE ELECTION SURVEYS CLOSES AFTER ADMITTING ‘SOCIAL EXPERIMENT’ "These people are absolute scumbags," veteran Democratic strategist and former Kamala Harris advisor Mike Nellis told Fox News Digital. "They can try to claim that they have some moral high ground here, but they lied about their polling data, got caught, and are freaking out because they've committed fraud." "The people responsible for this should be run out of American politics, and if they can be, they should be prosecuted to the full extent of the law," Nellis said. He added that both Democrats and Republicans, as well as the media, should reflect on how polling is verified "because there's likely other people that are doing things like this." TOP ELECTION SCHEMES ROILING KEY MIDTERM RACES AS BOTH PARTIES ACCUSE RIVALS OF TRICKERY Independent outlet FiftyPlusOne said it was investigating Wedgewood when it had released its statement. Co-founder G. Elliott Morris wrote on X, "We were investigating Wedgewood for faking their data and emailed them for comment this morning, ahead of publishing the findings tomorrow. They are trying to cover up their fraud with the 'we were doing a social experiment' excuse." Former Obama staffer Tommy Vietor said on X that Wedgewood's actions amounted to "lying and fraud." A group called "Wedgewood Polls" had also previously created a GoFundMe to raise money for polling in Nebraska's gubernatorial and Senate races. It raised $500 of its intended $5,000. "I know they crowdfunded, I believe, a good chunk of their polls," Nellis told Fox News Digital. "Are they going to return that money? And if not, are they going to be prosecuted?" FOX NEWS POLL: IT’S A LONE STAR SENATE SHOWDOWN BETWEEN TALARICO AND PAXTON Other Wedgewood surveys showed Democrats with significant edges over Republicans in states like Texas, where a July Wedgewood poll showed James Talarico leading state Attorney General Ken Paxton among Hispanics by 64% to 30%. Republicans, including President Donald Trump, have long heaped doubt on the veracity of polls. Polls notably showed former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton with an edge over Trump in 2016 — far from the actual result. And with the fight for control of Congress coming to a head in November, every data point is being scrutinized as political tea leaves. articles.title: Greta Thunberg joins Paris protests, underscoring radical three-way alliance
articles.summary: Greta Thunberg urged followers to mobilize for Paris protests days before demonstrations turned violent, joining a vast network of 54 organizations.
articles.body: Climate activist Greta Thunberg has joined French agitators, lending her "How dare you?" indignation to demonstrations that began over education grievances but soon devolved into violent, migrant-driven riots. In a video posted to her Instagram, Thunberg encouraged agitators to attend what became a clash between rioters, law enforcement and local business owners – calling on her followers to support the cause. "French students are out continuously facing extreme police brutality just for asking for their basic rights. And now it’s time for us to step up because they cannot carry this alone," Thunberg said. "They are showing the world, leading by example, what it looks like when young people are stepping up when the system at large is neglecting them systematically." GRETA THUNBERG JOINS MASSIVE FRENCH STUDENT PROTESTS AS CARS BURN, POLICE FIRE TEAR GAS "We are asking all of you to contribute with what you can, support them out on the streets, donate and come to the mobilization on Oct. 17," she added. The video was highlighted by the Al Jazeera Media Network on X, which noted Thunberg’s use of the phrase "bismillah, c’est les ténèbres," which translates to "In the name of God, it’s darkness." The phrase has become a slogan for protesters in France. TEEN'S HAND BLOWN OFF BY POLICE GRENADE DURING FRENCH STUDENT PROTESTS: REPORT While Thunberg is most notably known for her climate advocacy, describing herself as an "autistic & bipolar climate justice activist," she has been vocal on the conflict between Israel and Gaza. Last year, the 23-year-old activist attempted to reach Gaza by joining the Global Sumud Flotilla, demanding a humanitarian corridor before being intercepted and detained by Israeli authorities. Days after Thunberg’s social media post calling for mobilization in Paris, she collaborated with the Palestinian Youth Movement in a separate post that defined "the genocidal Israeli army" as "the killers of children." Watchdogs have noted a rise in the "red-green-green alliance," an ideological overlap between three elements: communist movements, characterized by the color red; Islamist activism, described as green; and environmental protest groups, also symbolized as green. The result is that the same loose group of activists and organizations support a wide array of seemingly unconnected causes. In June 2024, protesters gathered outside Citibank headquarters in New York City under the banner that "Climate Justice Means Free Palestine." GLOBAL 'CHAOS INC' GROWS TO 101 GROUPS WITH PLANS FOR NEW ROUNDS OF DEMONSTRATIONS As Thunberg, who became an international darling of the Left in 2019, when she lectured grownups at the UN Climate Action Summit, called on her followers to join the French protests, a network of global communist parties and revolutionary groups also prepared to take to the streets. With Palestinian flags flying alongside student-backed organizations in Paris, the "red-green-green" came into light. A Fox News Digital investigation has identified 54 organizations and movements behind "Chaos Inc." in France's October student protests and their wider network of supporters and international amplifiers, including communist parties, revolutionary socialist groups, labor unions, environmental activists, Muslim student advocates, Palestinian-solidarity organizations and international media outlets. COULD FRANCE'S RIOTS HAPPEN HERE? EXPERTS SEE PARALLELS IN SOCIALISM, IMMIGRATION — AND KEY DIFFERENCES Of the 54 organizations identified in the October protest ecosystem, 16 — or only about one in three — are student or youth organizations, including communist youth groups and a Muslim student association. The remaining 38 include adult-led communist groups, labor unions, political parties, revolutionary-left organizations, advocacy groups and international propaganda outlets. Fox News Digital also identified organizations within the Neville Roy Singham network, including Tricontinental, CodePink and BreakThrough News, a New York-based media outlet, which promoted coverage of the weekend's mayhem in France with the headline: "ANTI-MACRON PROTESTS ROCK FRANCE." CODEPINK LAUNCHES CHINA TOUR AS GRAND JURY INVESTIGATION INTO SINGHAM NETWORK FUNDING CONTINUES Singham, a 72-year-old American now living in Shanghai, China, sold his tech company for an estimated $785 million in 2017, and has since funneled $278 million into a broad network of nonprofits. These groups regularly organize and participate in anti-ICE, anti-Israel and pro-Iran demonstrations. Thunberg’s main vessel for activism, Fridays For Future, was not identified as an organizer, despite her call on social media to mobilize. The group's funding sources and practices are unclear, although Thunberg travels the globe advocating for various causes. For her 2019 UN speech, in which she uttered her trademark "How dare you?" indictment, the then-16-year-old arrived aboard a yacht powered by wind, with solar panels and water-driven generators to provide electricity. Thunberg was born in Stockholm, the daughter of Malena Ernman, a successful opera singer, and Svante Thunberg, an actor and producer. Diagnosed with Asperger's syndrome as a young teenager, she has described her autism as a "superpower." articles.title: Justice Department IG refuses to investigate botched Reflecting Pool case after Trump’s false vandalism claims
articles.summary: The Justice Department’s inspector general is refusing to investigate what went wrong with the botched criminal case against former Olympic canoeist David Hearn over damage at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, including whether there was any criminality on prosecutors’ parts, Hearn’s legal team said.
articles.body: The Justice Department’s inspector general is refusing to investigate what went wrong with the botched criminal case against former Olympic canoeist David Hearn over damage at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, including whether there was any criminality on prosecutors’ parts, Hearn’s legal team said. In a letter Wednesday to Inspector General Don R. Berthiaume, Hearn’s attorneys asked his office to reconsider its decision because of evidence of “numerous potential criminal violations — possible crimes committed solely by DOJ personnel, as well as crimes committed jointly by DOJ” employees and personnel from the Department of Interior. The inspector general’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Hearn’s attorneys had previously asked the watchdog to investigate “the incompetence and wrongdoing” of Justice Department employees, writing that the “sprint to charge Mr. Hearn mirrored the rushed renovation” of the Reflecting Pool itself. Hearn was charged in July with causing felony damage to President Donald Trump’s renovations of the Reflecting Pool. Trump had blamed the damage at the pool on Hearn and other “vandals.” U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro’s office moved to dismiss the case at the end of July, saying it had found the damage was “the result of flawed installation by the contractor, Atlantic Industrial Coatings.” A judge later tossed the case and barred the government from trying to charge Hearn again. Hearn’s attorneys contend he never should have been charged in the first place. They allege that the evidence shows prosecutors rushed to bring the case, despite already having evidence in their possession showing that Hearn’s putting his hands in the pool did not cause “any harm or monetary loss” — necessary elements of the felony he was charged with. They also cited an incident in the grand jury proceeding where a witness for the government “testified — truthfully — that the repairs were needed regardless of any actions by Mr. Hearn, that the witness did not know whether Mr. Hearn damaged the Reflecting Pool lining in any way, and that the witness could not quantify any incremental cost of repair caused by Mr. Hearn’s actions.” “Evidently disappointed with the testimony and realizing that it was fatal to its case, the government appears to have caused the witness to change that testimony,” the letter said. “After a 21-minute off-the record break, the witness returned to the stand and — after previously being unable to testify that Mr. Hearn caused any monetary damage whatsoever — the witness now testified that the damage was ‘definitely’ $1,000 or more,” the threshold needed to bring a felony charge. The letter also said the inspector general needs to investigate “whether prosecutors knowingly caused the witness to change his testimony on the magnitude-of-loss issue and to provide the false testimony the government needed to be able to charge a felony.” It also asked the inspector general to look into Pirro’s public comments about the case, which it said were prejudicial. “It is now undisputed — by everyone except President Trump —that Mr. Hearn should never have been arrested and certainly should not have been indicted. The OIG must now investigate whether the DOJ personnel responsible for this travesty engaged in misconduct that violated Mr. Hearn’s civil rights,” the letter says. Hearn’s attorneys first asked the inspector general to investigate the case earlier this month. The new letter said the IG responded that it would not open an investigation and the matter was one for the department’s Office of Professional Responsibility, which has authority to investigate “certain categories of misconduct committed by DOJ lawyers.” Hearn’s lawyers noted that office does not have criminal jurisdiction and has been gutted by the Trump administration, with the number of personnel cut in half. The “plain fact is that OPR is no longer a fully functioning entity capable of conducting rigorous oversight. Recent reporting has documented that the number of new OPR investigations is at a 20-year low at the same time as the number of complaints is spiraling to unprecedented levels,” the letter says, adding that if the inspector general doesn’t step in, “the investigation will simply not take place.” The letter said the Interior Department inspector general’s office is investigating Hearn’s allegations about their personnel. Trump fired 18 inspectors general upon his return to office last year, including that of the Interior Department. Inspectors general are typically considered to be independent figures within government agencies, and are expected to investigate allegations of waste, fraud and abuse of power within their departments. The president said at the time of the firings that “I did it because it’s a very common thing to do,” despite the abrupt terminations being highly unusual. “Some people thought that some were unfair or were not doing the job. It’s a very standard thing to do,” Trump said.

articles.title: Newsom spars with Trump-appointed prosecutor over 20,000 suspected noncitizens on voter rolls
articles.summary: Gavin Newsom and Bill Essayli clashed over noncitizen voting after an LA County official said the registrar cannot verify voter citizenship.
articles.body: Governor Gavin Newsom and Bill Essayli, a Trump-appointed federal prosecutor in California, sparred on social media this week about whether the state is doing enough to prevent noncitizens from voting. Essayli, the first assistant U.S. attorney for California's Central District, surfaced a court document filed Tuesday in which a Los Angeles County election official said the registrar's office "is not equipped or authorized to verify voter citizenship because it does not independently house citizenship-related information beyond the voter attestation." The official, Monica Flores, made the declaration as part of a Justice Department lawsuit seeking to force California to verify the citizenship of more than 20,000 people the federal government believes are likely noncitizens who were sent mail ballots ahead of this year's midterm elections. Essayli called Flores' statement a "massive concession" that shows election officials take voters' word on whether they are a citizen. STATE DEPARTMENT CONSIDERS SHARING PASSPORT RECORDS FOR VOTER CITIZENSHIP CHECKS "American citizens’ votes are being diluted in California," Essayli wrote. In response, Newsom's press office account on X said California adheres to a 1993 federal law that requires people registering to vote through the DMV to swear under penalty of perjury that they are eligible, including that they are U.S. citizens. Similar attestation requirements apply to federal mail-in voter registration forms. "May want to brush up on your election law before tweeting," Newsom's office wrote in a jab at Essayli. "Perhaps Second Assistant is more apt from now on?" Essayli fired back by citing two federal statutes that make it unlawful for noncitizens to vote in federal elections. ‘RAW MATERIAL FOR ELECTION FRAUD’: EXPERT FLAGS VOTER-ROLL PROBLEMS FAR BEYOND ONE STATE The public spat highlighted the central dispute in the lawsuit against California: whether the state should take additional steps to verify the citizenship of voters when the federal government flags potential issues with the rolls. According to the Justice Department's complaint, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) cross-checked California voter registration records with federal immigration data. That investigative process, described by DOJ lawyers as "preliminary," yielded a list of more than 20,000 registered voters federal investigators identified as likely noncitizens. California voters were mailed ballots beginning Oct. 1. In its initial complaint filed Oct. 15, the Justice Department asked a federal court to require California to set aside mail ballots associated with people on the list until their citizenship could be verified. Flores, an official with the LA County Registrar's Office, argued that doing so is now virtually impossible because once a ballot's signature is verified, it is removed from its identifying envelope and processed alongside hundreds of thousands of others. DOJ OFFICIAL DEFENDS TRUMP'S NONCITIZEN VOTER PROBE ON '60 MINUTES,' ACCUSES SHOW OF EDITING OUT HER ANSWERS As of Tuesday, the county has processed 331,000 ballots, according to Flores' statement in court. She also pointed out that the registrar's office is "not an investigative agency," adding that she was unaware of "any state or federal law granting it investigative authority." Nonetheless, staff from the registrar's office reviewed a sample of 200 records from the Justice Department list that had LA County addresses. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "The October list is unreliable: 112 of the 200 records correspond to registrations that are canceled or inactive," according to Flores' statement. "Of the voters where birthplace was meaningfully reported, 38.9% indicate that they were born in the United States, which is strong evidence of citizenship; and 71.2% of the records have no voting history." In a statement to Fox News, Essayli said these reported numbers "are meaningless because, by their own admission, they have no way to verify anyone's citizenship status or their birthplace." There are indications that the Justice Department list does contain at least some individuals who could have broken the law. On Monday, the Justice Department charged 28 individuals off that list, all lawful permanent residents, with making false statements on naturalization applications and fraudulently registering to vote. Most of them cast unlawful ballots in elections, officials said.

articles.title: El-Sayed's past Muslim Brotherhood comments raise red flags as he eyes powerful role
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed's past support for Muslim Brotherhood protesters in Egypt faces sharp criticism from Senate Republicans on the Foreign Relations Committee.
articles.body: Abdul El-Sayed’s past support for Muslim Brotherhood protesters in Egypt is raising eyebrows in Congress after a former staffer for the left-wing Michigan Senate candidate says he's angling for a seat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee if elected in November. Two Republican panel members said there is no place on the committee for "radical views" held by El-Sayed, who has associated with controversial streamer Hasan Piker but has attempted during his bid for office to distance himself from the socialist arm of the Democratic Party. "A man with ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, who cheered their takeover of Egypt 15 years ago, and who campaigns with people saying America deserved 9/11, should not come anywhere near the U.S. Senate — and especially not the Foreign Relations Committee," Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, who serves on the power panel, told Fox News Digital. Sen. Dave McCormick, R-Pa., another member of the committee, responded to the controversy on X over the weekend. TRUMP LINKS MICHIGAN SENATE CANDIDATE ABDUL EL-SAYED TO MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD: 'HE'S A CON MAN' "El-Sayed says he’s running on affordability, so why does he want a seat on @SenateForeign?" McCormick wrote. "I sit on that committee, and someone with El-Sayed's radical views has no business on it." McCormick’s post came in response to a report by The Midwesterner that featured comments from Jordan Domingue, who worked as El-Sayed’s security chief during his 2018 campaign for Michigan governor. "It is extremely difficult to comprehend how dangerous this can be if he is elected," Domingue wrote on X. "It’s especially troubling knowing that despite no foreign policy experience, he REALLY wants a seat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee." In 2011, while working as an assistant professor at Columbia University, El-Sayed wrote an op-ed for The Huffington Post urging the Obama administration to support protesters associated with Egypt’s Muslim Brotherhood. ABDUL EL-SAYED GROWS AGITATED WITH REPORTER AFTER BEING PRESSED ON FAMILY'S ALLEGED MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD TIES El-Sayed argued that supporting the protesters was in the U.S. interest and wrote that even if the Muslim Brotherhood overthrew Egypt’s government, the resulting state would not necessarily resemble Iran. "It is in America’s interest to support Egyptian protesters’ efforts to achieve the ability to speak their mind and have a say in how they are governed," El-Sayed wrote . "If the U.S. truly wants to be the beacon of justice and liberty that it claims it does, it would behoove the Obama administration to fall decisively behind the protesters in Egypt." In a recent town hall, however, El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrant parents, said he does disavow the Muslim Brotherhood. His campaign did not respond to Fox News Digital’s request about his 2011 op-ed about protesters. The Muslim Brotherhood-backed government took power in Egypt in 2012 but was ousted by the military in 2013. 'POD SAVE AMERICA' HOSTS WARN EL-SAYED TO TONE DOWN 'CONDESCENSION' ON MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD QUESTIONS El-Sayed has throughout his campaign emphasized healthcare, lowering gas and grocery prices and addressing the cost-of-living crisis, as noted by McCormick in his post about the candidate's reported interest in the Foreign Relations Committee. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It shouldn’t be this hard to get by in the richest, most powerful country in the world," El-Sayed said during his primary campaign against Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., and state Sen. Mallory McMorrow. McCormick wonders why, given that context, El-Sayed would be gunning for a spot on a committee that deals solely with issues related to U.S. foreign relations.

articles.title: Manchin calls Schumer 'crazy' for trying to oust GOP senator in crucial Senate showdown
articles.summary: Joe Manchin called Chuck Schumer "crazy" for trying to unseat Susan Collins as he joined the Maine senator on the campaign trail in Lewiston.
articles.body: LEWISTON, MAINE – Former Sen. Joe Manchin, a longtime Democrat turned independent, took aim at Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer on Wednesday for trying to unseat Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, calling his former party leader's efforts "crazy" as he joined Collins on the campaign trail in her high-stakes re-election race. Collins, a moderate Republican who at times has voted against President Donald Trump and her party, is fighting for her political life as she runs for a sixth six-year term representing blue-leaning Maine in the Senate. She is the only GOP senator seeking re-election in a state Trump lost in the 2024 election. The race between Collins and Troy Jackson, a former state Senate president, is a top flip opportunity for Democrats as they try to win back the Senate majority from Republicans in the midterm elections. The latest public opinion polls indicate a margin-of-error showdown, and the latest Fox News Power Rankings rate the race as a toss-up, as do leading nonpartisan political handicappers the Cook Political Report, Inside Elections and Sabato's Crystal Ball. Manchin, who worked closely with Collins during his years in the Senate, was asked by Fox News Digital how his campaigning with his former colleague would sit with Schumer, the top Democrat in the chamber. DEMOCRATS THINK A BLUE WAVE IS BUILDING - HERE ARE THREE FACTORS THAT COULD STOP IT "Chuck Schumer would not be surprised of me being with my dear friend. There is no surprise there at all. I told him he was crazy in 2020 from working against her so hard and he’s crazy now to work against her," Manchin said, as he referred to unsuccessful efforts by Democrats to defeat Collins in her re-election six years ago, and their current push to oust her. Manchin emphasized, "This is not right. She is the soul of America. She is the soul of the Senate, and he knows he needs more Susan Collins, no matter what side of the aisle they’re on. This is ridiculous." Fox News Digital reached out to Schumer's political team and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee for a comment but did not receive a response at the time this story was published. A former West Virginia governor who served in the Senate from 2010 to 2025, Manchin frequently broke with his party, frustrating Democratic Presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden, as well as Schumer and other Senate Democratic leaders. As he works to oust Collins from the Senate, Jackson has repeatedly tried to anchor the senator to Trump, who has seen his approval ratings in Maine and across the country drop further underwater. DEMS SEE NEW CHANCES TO FLIP SENATE SEATS BUT GOP'S MASSIVE CASH ADVANTAGE AN OBSTACLE But Manchin said that Collins is "not a Trump senator. She's not a Republican senator or a Democrat senator. She's an American senator that represents her state of Maine ... the most independent minded person I've ever met." Collins noted that "Joe and I were part of every bipartisan initiative that passed the Senate and became law during the years that we worked together ... I just so enjoy our partnership in getting things done for Maine, for West Virginia and for America." Manchin and Collins spoke with reporters after meeting with restaurant workers and customers at Simones' Hot Dog Stand, a famed local eatery in downtown Lewiston that's been serving customers for a century. It was the first of two campaign stops in Maine's 2nd Congressional District, a key swing district. Collins and Jackson last week faced off on the debate stage for the fourth and final time. The senator used the debates to showcase how her Senate seniority has helped her deliver federal funding for Maine. Meanwhile, Jackson used the showdowns to position himself as an outsider who understands the struggles and frustrations of working-class voters. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Jackson won a special nominating convention in late July to claim the party's Senate nomination, which was left vacant after primary winner Graham Platner ended his campaign following allegations he raped a woman he previously dated. Platner denied the allegations but dropped out. Jackson, who earlier this year unsuccessfully ran for the Democratic gubernatorial nomination, had campaigned alongside Platner during the primary campaign. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Collins, meanwhile, has a history of surviving Democratic efforts to unseat her. Six years ago, she trailed Democratic challenger Sara Gideon, the Maine House speaker at the time, but Collins won re-election by nearly nine points while former President Joe Biden carried the state by a similar margin. Fox News' Kailey Schuyler contributed to this story.

articles.title: Vance warns Republicans not to complain about Ramaswamy ad featuring Amy Acton’s estranged mother
articles.summary: Vice President JD Vance on Wednesday warned Ohio Republicans not to break ranks over a controversial new ad from their gubernatorial nominee, Vivek Ramaswamy...
articles.body:
Vice President JD Vance on Wednesday warned Ohio Republicans not to break ranks over a controversial new ad from their gubernatorial nominee, Vivek Ramaswamy, that drew bipartisan criticism for featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent.

"Politics is a tough business, and my message to my fellow elected Republicans is if you actually believe in the things you say you believe in, stop whining about an advertisement and go win the race in 13 days," Vance said at a news conference in Cincinnati.

The initial video – which was shared widely on social media, including by the president's eldest son, Donald Trump Jr. – has been roiling the gubernatorial race since it first showed up on social media, bringing the abuse Democratic nominee Amy Acton said she suffered at the hands of her stepfather to the forefront.

In the video, Acton's mother urged voters not to support her daughter. Acton has said she has not seen her mother since she was about 12 years old, when the man her mother married abused her and faced criminal charges.

Democrats condemned the spot, and even some Republicans – including Nikki Haley and Meghan McCain – were critical. But Ohio Republicans have so far been quiet, and the remarks by Vance, a former senator from the state, appeared to be an attempt to keep the party in line during an especially fraught moment.

Asked about the ad at the news conference, Vance declined to weigh in on its appropriateness but said he was "a little bit disgusted" that some Republicans appeared more outraged about it than they are about Democrats and their policies.

Speaking later at a rally in Cincinnati that Ramaswamy attended, Vance brought up the ad on his own. He argued it was a justified response because Democrats have used "every dirty trick in the political book" against Ramaswamy.

"Now the media and the Democrats in the state of Ohio are obsessed because guess what? Vivek Ramaswamy had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is and calls Amy Acton a liar," Vance said.

Ramaswamy's campaign leaned into the controversy over the ad Tuesday night, announcing it would spend $4 million to run the spot.

"She's lied her entire life," Donna Arthur says in the minute-long spot. "My daughter needs help, and she can't help you if she needs help herself. People can change, but first they have to tell the truth, and my daughter still isn't doing that."

The video was first published on Monday night by an Ohio political blogger, D.J. Byrnes, who is known as "The Rooster." Byrnes told CNN he obtained the video from a voter who saw it as part of a poll and recorded it. On Tuesday morning, Acton's campaign released a statement from her brother, Philip Stearns, denouncing the video and linking it to Ramaswamy.

"It's not surprising that Vivek Ramaswamy has stooped to such a despicable low as to attempt to turn the sexual abuse Amy endured at twelve years old from our birth mother's husband into a political talking point," Stearns said. "After he was arrested and Amy and I were removed from their custody, our birth mother stayed married to Amy's rapist until he died."

Later Tuesday, Acton's campaign released a new ad featuring Stearns making similar points. "Shame on Vivek," he says in the spot.

Ad did not initially have political disclaimer

Ramaswamy's campaign initially did not confirm their involvement in the ad Tuesday, saying only that Ohioans "deserve to know" what Acton's mother says about her daughter. But later in the day, Ramaswamy confirmed, "It is an ad from our campaign."

The incendiary spot will run on TV and streaming platforms, according to a spokesperson for the Ramaswamy campaign, Connie Luck. Axios first reported the news.

When it first circulated, the video did not have the standard disclaimer that political ads carry saying who paid for or authorized them, nor did it show up Tuesday morning as a paid ad in the race on AdImpact, the political ad-tracking service.

And the first Ramaswamy campaign statement from Luck did not address whether it was responsible for the video. It suggested voters should consider the message from Acton's mother and repeated her attack, asserting that "we know that Amy Acton is a serial fabulist who has some serious problems with the truth that the public needs to be aware of before deciding who to entrust as governor."

The statement went on to argue that people who know Acton well — including "her own mother" — "are clearly warning Ohioans not to vote for her."

"Ohioans deserve to know that," Luck said.

An official with V-PAC, the main super PAC backing Ramaswamy, said it did not make the video. CNN has attempted to contact Arthur for more information about how the video came together.

Ramaswamy was heckled at a campaign event Tuesday evening by a person appearing to cite the viral video. Within seconds of Ramaswamy taking the stage at a Columbus-area town hall, an audience member rose up and began yelling at him, making a reference to "Amy Acton's mother" and the abuse that the candidate says she suffered from her mother's husband at a young age.

"Sir, if you want to be patient and you want to ask a question at the end, you're free to do that," Ramaswamy said as the man was escorted out. "Thank you for your contribution today."

Speaking with reporters after the event, Ramaswamy took responsibility for the ad and reiterated that voters should take into account what people who know Acton "well" are saying about her. He said he has never met the mother and that she was "not compensated" for the ad.

Acton herself weighed in during an interview with WOSU Public Media .

"It's awful to see her this way, and it's even more incredible to see that my opponent (Ramaswamy) has taken advantage of someone who's clearly not well, who is older, and this is totally in line with who he is," Acton said.

The ad drew criticism even from some Republicans. Haley, Ramaswamy's former rival in the 2024 presidential primary, said it was the latest evidence that Ramaswamy is "a bad guy."

"It's a shame he continues to get away with it," she wrote on X .

Meghan McCain, the daughter of the late Arizona GOP Sen. John McCain, said on X that the ad was "dastardly" and "never should have been created."

Sherrod Brown, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Ohio, said on X that the video was "disgusting" and that his opponent, GOP Sen. Jon Husted, should condemn it. The Democratic Governors Association said in a statement that the video was part of a "relentless smear campaign" that Ramaswamy has waged against Acton.

Acton and Ramaswamy are locked in one of the most competitive governor's races in the country, vying to replace term-limited Republican Mike DeWine. The ads in the race have been especially nasty, fueling a controversial decision by Acton to decline to debate Ramaswamy. Republican candidates in the state are preparing for a statewide bus tour starting Friday.

Husted's campaign has not responded to a request for comment on the ad. DeWine's office also has not commented, even though he has defended Acton earlier in the campaign.

A member of DeWine's Cabinet, Lydia Mihalik, said Tuesday on X that the ad crossed a line.

"We can disagree on plenty of things without losing our sense of decency," said Mihalik, director of the state's Department of Development. "I don't have to agree with Amy Acton's politics to believe that exploiting someone's childhood trauma is wrong."

Nick Owens, a Republican activist in Ohio, told CNN the ad is "frankly despicable" and would help Acton raise "a lot of money." Owens, who calls himself a lifelong Republican, is a former county GOP chair in the state who's been organizing opposition to data centers.

Acton, the former Ohio public health director, has spoken before about her estrangement from her mother and hardscrabble childhood. In a 2019 interview with the Youngstown Vindicator , she said her mother married a man when she was between ages 9 and 12 who abused her and who faced criminal charges. The family was living in a tent at a campground outside Youngstown at the time.

According to legal documents provided by the Acton campaign, Acton's allegations against her stepfather emerged in July of 1978 when her father testified to police his daughter was sexually abused by her stepfather. A day later, her stepfather was arrested for rape. He pleaded not guilty but was indicted by a grand jury in September of that year. By October, prosecutors asked for a warrant for his arrest. In the early 1980s, one record shows authorities were still looking for him, but there is no record of any further action in the case.

"I was lucky that it got bad enough, because it got me out of there," Acton told the Vindicator.

She said the last time she saw her mother was at the courthouse when she tried to give her a kiss and Acton rejected her.

This story has been updated with additional information.

CNN's Lauren Fox and Kit Maher contributed to this report.

articles.title: New Mexico sues Epstein attorney and accountant, accuses them of hiding sex trafficking operation
articles.summary: New Mexico’s attorney general sued Jeffrey Epstein’s attorney and accountant on Wednesday, accusing them of concealing his sex trafficking operation at a Santa Fe-area ranch where the disgraced financier once entertained guests.
articles.body: ALBUQUERQUE, N.M. — New Mexico’s attorney general sued Jeffrey Epstein’s attorney and accountant on Wednesday, accusing them of concealing his sex trafficking operation at a Santa Fe-area ranch where the disgraced financier once entertained guests. The lawsuit seeks to stop Darren Indyke and Richard Kahn from accepting any payments from Epstein’s estate. Attorney General Raul Torrez also accused Indyke and Kahn of being aware of sexual abuse of girls and young women at Epstein’s Zorro Ranch. Indyke worked as Epstein’s attorney for roughly two decades. Both he and Kahn have testified in a congressional committee that they did not know about Epstein’s abuse, though Torrez has a different view. He said Epstein’s estate holds more than $100 million, and that Indyke and Kahn “stand to benefit substantially” unless a court intervenes. “Those resources rightfully belong in the hands of survivors,” the attorney general said, referring to victims of Epstein’s abuse. Epstein purchased the ranch in Stanley, New Mexico, a sparsely populated ranching community about 30 miles (48 kilometers) south of Santa Fe, in 1993. He built a 26,700-square-foot mansion with a sprawling courtyard, a living room roughly the size of the average American home, and a private airstrip and helipad. Epstein never faced charges in New Mexico, though the state attorney general’s office in 2019 confirmed that it was investigating and planned to forward its findings to federal authorities in New York. Hector Balderas, who was attorney general at the time, said the state’s outdated laws failed to protect children from abuse. The property was sold by Epstein’s estate in 2023 — with proceeds going toward creditors — to the family of Don Huffines, a Republican recently appointed Texas’ state comptroller. Huffines said in a social media post the property has been renamed San Rafael Ranch and that his family plans to operate a Christian retreat there.
